Technology Commercialization Fund The Technology Commercialization Fund (TCF) is a U.S. Department of Energy program that helps move innovations developed at DOE National Laboratories, plants, and sites into the marketplace. Established by Congress in the Energy Policy Act of 2005, TCF invests millions of dollars each year to bridge the gap between research and commercial application. The program supports partnerships between DOE facilities and industry, universities, and other organizations to advance technologies with strong market potential. By sharing costs with private and public partners, TCF strengthens the lab-to-market pipeline, fosters collaboration, and ensures that federally funded research delivers tangible benefits to the nation’s economy and energy security. The Tees Rivers Trust have found 12 large eels by fyke netting, a method of catching eels with a cylindrical net, around the River Tees catchment. The team managed to electronically tag 10 of them and the largest was 60cm (23ins) in length and weighted 435g (0.9lbs). Project manager Ellie Ward said the eels caught this year were not as large as usual and were "harder to catch". The team has been searching for "silver" eels which have finished maturing and are preparing to head back out to the Sargasso Sea near Bermuda. Ward said: "European eels start to migrate downstream during autumn and winter, when river discharges increase. "We suspect that low flows in summer that have continued into autumn have contributed to low catch rates so far this year." pages.description: Nikkolas Smith, the bestselling illustrator, has a new children's book that takes a look at the innovative, creative dawn of our species.
pages.text: Telling the story of humanity’s origins in Africa—this time, for kids | National Geographic HISTORY & CULTURE Telling the story of humanity’s origins in Africa—this time, for kids Nikkolas Smith, the bestselling illustrator, has a new children's book that takes a look at the innovative, creative dawn of our species. The illustrator Nikkolas Smith, surrounded by his original canvas paintings for his new children's book, The History of We. Photograph By Vanessa Crocini By Kyndall Cunningham Published June 11, 2025 You’ve probably heard that we can all trace our roots back to Africa. It’s a fact that most people learn about briefly in a history class or find out through 23andMe. Still, this shared origin story often feels like a blip in our consciousness compared to other time periods. It’s a commonality we’re willing to acknowledge but not always explore. Picture-book author and film illustrator Nikkolas Smith fills in this curiosity gap with his latest book, The History of We , which he both wrote and illustrated. The self-described “artivist” has dedicated much of his career to rendering crucial moments and people in Black history through expressive paintings, from portraits of George Floyd and Breonna Taylor to a comic-book treatment of the Obamas. One of his most well-known projects is The 1619 Project: Born on the Water, the children’s adaptation of the New York Times venture led by Nikole-Hannah Jones, which he illustrated. With The History of We , Smith continues this tradition of documenting Black history in a way that’s accessible, honest, and completely mesmerizing.

Un preparador de declaraciones de impuestos remunerado es principalmente responsable de la precisión fundamental de su declaración y, por ley, tiene el requisito de firmar la declaración e incluir el número de identificación tributaria del preparador remunerado (PTIN, por sus siglas en inglés) en la declaración. Aunque el preparador de declaraciones de impuestos siempre firma la declaración, usted es responsable en última instancia de la exactitud de cada partida que se incluya en su declaración. Get our Newsletter! Like many birds, domestic turkeys, including this group at the Smithsonian's National Zoo in Washington, D.C., are social animals. Smithsonian/Brett Kuxhausen 1. Humans have been raising turkeys for thousands of years. Although indigenous peoples in North America have hunted wild turkeys since the end of the last Ice Age, the animals were first domesticated in Mexico around 2,000 years ago. Dinner wasn’t the original goal: archaeological evidence suggests turkeys were initially kept so their feathers could be used in clothing and ceremonial regalia. By A.D. 500, people were raising turkeys in what is now the United States too, judging by archaeological remains from caves in Arizona and New Mexico. Even so, those weren’t the birds that English settlers ate in the Thirteen Colonies. The domestic turkey descends from a southern Mexican bird that the Spanish took home in the 1500s. The birds then spread through Europe, and colonists brought them back across the Atlantic. The bird’s English name may reflect this long-distance trade: turkeys are thought to have reached England along winding trading routes that first passed through the country of Turkey. 2. Tetanus: Causes and How It Spreads For Everyone Sept. 10, 2026 Español Key points Tetanus spores from the environment enter the body through cuts or wounds. Tetanus doesn't spread from person to person. It is possible to have tetanus infection more than once. Prevent tetanus by staying up to date with vaccinations and seeking appropriate care after a wound. Causes Bacteria live in the environment Spores of Clostridium tetani are common in the environment, including soil, dust, and manure. The spores develop into bacteria when they enter the body. Common exposures The spores can get into someone's body through broken skin, usually through injuries. Tetanus bacteria are more likely to infect certain breaks in the skin, including: Wounds contaminated with dirt, feces (poop), or saliva (spit) Puncture wounds (wounds caused by an object, like a nail or needle) Injuries with dead tissue (e.g., burns, crush injuries, frostbite) Dead tissue is a concern because it can promote bacteria growth. For centuries, the permafrost protected the graves of men who hunted whales in the Arctic. But coastal erosion and melting ice now threaten to decay their remains. Lise Loktu and Espen Olsen, Governor of Svalbard. By Kat Long Published July 28, 2026 More than 300 years ago, young men from all over Western Europe boarded ships bound for the Arctic. Under the unceasing light of polar summer, in a landscape of rock and ice, they hunted bowhead whales in the waters surrounding the Svalbard archipelago. The work was brutal; the wind unrelenting. Many never made it home. They were buried in whalers’ graveyards, fully dressed in their woolen jackets and knitted hats. Their shallow graves were marked with mounds of stones. pages.description: Scientists call the events permafrost detachment slides. Instead of thawing from the top down, these landslides seem to originate from a weakened base
pages.text: Thawing Permafrost May Have Created a New Type of Landslide, Which Could Become More Common as the World Warms Skip to main content A scar left by the 2018 Redstone River permafrost landslide, one of the two events investigated in the new study. Adapted from J. M. Young et al., Geophysical Research Letters , 2026 In 2017 and 2018, a pair of strange landslides moved huge masses of rock and dirt in Canada’s Northwest Territories. The events occurred in the central Mackenzie Valley, and one of them even dammed a river and created a lake . The two natural disasters are part of a new class of landslides scientists are calling “permafrost detachment slides” in a study published in the journal Geophysical Research Letters in September. They may have been partially triggered by severe wildfires that occurred in 1995, which destabilized the ground and allowed the base of the permafrost to thaw. What’s more, these events may become more common as the planet continues to warm. “It’s a very dramatic manifestation of the changing climate,” says study co-author Joseph Young , a geoscientist who conducted the work at the University of Alberta in Canada, to Matt Simon at Grist . “They’ve only started happening in the last 10, 15 years, and it’s a very drastic and abrupt change in the landscape.” Young and his colleagues began the study after seeing something strange in the Northwest Territories in 2019. While conducting field research, they spotted large landslide scars in valleys that they knew were stable permafrost , or permanently frozen earth, reports Stephanie Pappas for Live Science

Wikimedia Commons One hundred and fifty-nine years ago, slave traders stole Lorna Gail Woods ’ great-great grandfather from what is now Benin in West Africa. Her ancestor, Charlie Lewis, was brutally ripped from his homeland, along with 109 other Africans, and brought to Alabama on the Clotilda , the last known slave ship to arrive in the United States. Today, researchers confirmed that the remains of that vessel, long rumored to exist but elusive for decades, have been found along the Mobile River, near 12 Mile Island and just north of the Mobile Bay delta. “The excitement and joy is overwhelming,” says Woods, in a voice trembling with emotion. She is 70 years old now. But she’s been hearing stories about her family history and the ship that tore them from their homeland since she was a child in Africatown, a small community just north of Mobile founded by the Clotilda ’s survivors after the Civil War. pages.text: The Artisans Trying to Bring Back Neolithic Fashion | National Geographic Premium HISTORY & CULTURE The Artisans Trying to Bring Back Neolithic Fashion A growing community of craftspeople are trying to build knowledge of ancient clothing—by making it themselves. Historical craft specialist Vasi Birchwood recreates fashion from the Neolithic period on her Youtube channel. This outfit is one of her creations. The jacket is made of deer skin, stitched with deer skin cord and a bone awl, and adorned with moose teeth. The shirt underneath the jacket is made of undyed linen, hand stitched with linen thread. The skirt is made of deer skin and decorated with braided hemp strings. Photo Illustration: NGM Staff; Source Photos for Illustration: Vasi Birchwood By Starre Vartan Published November 2, 2026 Around the fire, no one seems especially bothered by the rain. Some people duck beneath bark shelters to continue twisting cordage from plant fibers. Others cook foraged plants or work leather while steam rises from damp clothing. A few wander into the drizzle to gather more wood before returning to the warmth of the flames. Among them is historical craft specialist and YouTube educator Vasi Birchwood . For Birchwood, weather isn't an inconvenience so much as another participant in this meeting of experiential archeologists and craft experts in Northern Germany. That shift in perspective is just one of the many ways she does more than dress like a Neolithic person at these gatherings. pages.text: The Astronomical Problem of Space Junk Skip to main content Illustration by Emily Lankiewicz / Images by Samantha Lawler / NASA / smspsy via Adobe Stock and public domain We have launched all manner of satellite and machinery into low-Earth orbit. But what goes up must come down. Most often, these items burn up in the atmosphere upon re-entry, which isn’t good for air quality or the ozone layer. But not everything incinerates — and increasing amounts of debris are hurtling back toward Earth and landing in backyards and farm fields. Falling detritus disrupts air travel and risks collision with infrastructure and people on the ground. There are those who argue that additional regulation is required around the launching and de-orbiting of these materials. In this episode, host Ari Daniel speaks with astronomer Samantha Lawler and Smithsonian contributing writer Dan Falk about space junk and the concern among researchers that it is becoming a growing threat to public safety. The continent of North America has been inhabited by humans for at least 16,500 years. As early as the 1500s, early settlers and European thinkers were interested in discovering how humans had come to populate North and South America. One theory suggested the migration of Norsemen across Greenland into North America. Another theory proposed the island of Atlantis as the origins of human life in the New World. Yet another idea proposed that the inhabitants had generated out of mud. However, by the early 1800s, scientists and theorists began discussing the possibility of a land bridge that had spanned between Asia and North America thousands of years ago. For all of human history people have looked up to the inky blackness of night and marvelled at the stars. Yet true darkness just isn’t something Europeans experience in the same way anymore due to artificial light illuminating the night sky. Light pollution can disrupt sleep and circadian rhythms, affect wildlife and ecosystems, and contribute to unnecessary energy use and carbon emissions. With this in mind, it’s no surprise more of us than ever are swapping chasing the sun for chasing the stars instead. DarkSky International is a non-profit organisation that certifies destinations around the world for the quality of their night skies, their approach to artificial lighting, conservation efforts and long-term commitment to protecting darkness. pages.text: The best night-sky apps, according to park rangers and aurora chasers | National Geographic TRAVEL The best night-sky apps, according to park rangers and aurora chasers Hoping for a glimpse of the Milky Way? These user-friendly apps help stargazers learn more about objects in the sky, check visibility for prime Milky Way viewing, or even locate the International Space Station. These apps and recommendations from experts will help you learn about what you're seeing when you gaze up at the night sky. Dan Zaffra By Amy Brecount White Published January 14, 2026 Where was I when a magenta aurora borealis could be seen as far south as Florida? Indoors and not paying enough attention. Accessibility Description (ABA/ADA) There are limited facilities at The Box Recreation Area. Campsites are primitive, and visitors need to be able to walk for several yards across uneven dirt roads that lead uphill to access. The trail leading down into The Box is made of dirt, goes downhill, and dotted with rocks that may be a tripping hazard. pages.text: The Case for Buying Kefir Over Yogurt | National Geographic Premium HEALTH The Case for Buying Kefir Over Yogurt The centuries-old drink is a microbiome powerhouse, packed with health benefits. In addition to its gut health benefits, kefir is also a good source of calcium, vitamin D, and protein. Rebecca Hale, NGM Staff By Meryl Davids Landau Published November 5, 2026 While kefir may have started as a potential accident centuries ago, scientists studying the increasingly popular fermented milk drink believe it may just live up to the hype (even if its origin stories likely do not). A review of more than two dozen human clinical trials published in March 2026 in the journal Healthcare concludes that consuming this probiotic-rich beverage offers small but meaningful improvements to the gut, the cardiovascular system, and even the mouth lining (which, like the intestines, is home to numerous good and bad bacteria). Kefir, the review states, is “a functional fermented milk beverage that can support human health on multiple levels.” Adding to the evidence are the test tube and animal studies documenting expanded microbe colonies in the gastrointestinal tract post consumption, along with other benefits such as improved cholesterol, immunity, and blood glucose regulation, a different review reported in February 2026 . ( Probiotics, Prebiotics, Postbiotics. pages.text: The Colonies Come Together, Lesson 2 | Crash Course: American Revolution | National Geographic Premium HISTORY & CULTURE CRASH COURSE The Colonies Come Together Lesson 2: Outraged by the Intolerable Acts, the Colonies decided to meet in Philadelphia on September 5, 1774, for the first Continental Congress. The crown’s harsh laws had backfired, reminding colonists that they were at the mercy of the whims of King George and his Parliament. Twelve of the Colonies sent delegates to Carpenters’ Hall, a brick building in central Philadelphia. Georgia declined to participate, wary of alienating the British as it faced threats from nearby Native American nations. East Florida and West Florida, then in the hands of the British, also did not participate. The First Continental Congress convened at Carpenters’ Hall in Philadelphia—a setting associated with common Americans—in September 1774 to debate how to respond to the Intolerable Acts that placed Massachusetts under military rule. Ann Broder, UCG/Universal Images Group via Getty Images Fifty-six delegates arrived in total, including George Washington and John Adams from Virginia and Massachusetts, respectively. Though the delegates were galvanized by the injustice of the Intolerable Acts, many still considered themselves loyal subjects of the British crown. pages.text: The Complicated Social Life of a Tyrannosaurus Rex | National Geographic SCIENCE Why Everything We Thought We Knew About T. Rex is Getting … Messier Fossil evidence has shifted our view of T. rex from a complete loner tyrant into a more nuanced carnivore. Scarred skulls, scraped ground, and fossilized trackways suggest adult tyrannosaurs lived largely solitary lives, like modern big cats, but also gathered in communal display arenas to woo potential mates. GERD LUDWIG, National Geographic Image Collection By Riley Black Published October 8, 2026 Every time I’m in New York, I have to visit her. She’s always waiting in the same place, standing on the fourth floor of the American Museum of Natural History, grinning so wide that her teeth gleam under the bright lights. Experts know her as AMNH 5027. I know her as the first T yrannosaurus rex I ever met. Before the discovery of “Sue,” “Stan,” “Scotty,” and many other famous skeletons of Earth’s last great carnivorous dinosaur, AMNH 5027 was the icon. The partial skeleton was the first T . rex to include a complete skull – only slightly smushed. It left no doubt that the dinosaur was an impressive flesh-ripper, reconstructed with jaws agape when the museum’s paleontologists assembled real bones and casts in the world’s first great introduction to the dinosaur. (And, when Michael Crichton’s Jurassic Park needed a skeletal dinosaur for the cover, AMNH 5027 was the model.) In 2014 just four tigers remained in India’s Similipal Tiger Reserve. The only male, T12 (pictured), was born with a rare genetic mutation that left him with a predominantly black coat. As T12 helped repopulate Similipal, his dark coat showed up in his offspring—raising serious concerns over inbreeding. Story, photographs, and video by Prasenjeet Yadav Published September 15, 2025 It took 50 days of searching before the jungle revealed its biggest secret to us. Fifty days of jostling along gravel roads in the Similipal Tiger Reserve , in India’s eastern state of Odisha, scanning between trees in the semi-evergreen forest, hoping for a glimpse of an elusive tiger called T12, whose striking appearance has made him a symbol of a population at a perilous crossroads. My partner in the quest, Raghu Purti, a staffer with the regional forest department, had never set eyes on T12. Most of his colleagues had only ever seen the tiger in images from camera traps set up to study animal movements throughout the reserve. Jane Rogers September 3, 2021 Get our Newsletter! Get our Newsletter! Photograph by Jane Rogers. (NMAH) About a month after the terrorist attacks on 9/11, I received a phone call from a colleague asking if I wanted to take a trip up to New York City to collect objects from Ground Zero for the museum. Although now a curator with the sports collection, at the time I was the curator of the fire and rescue collections and he thought I would like to collect from the fire and rescue personnel on site. I hesitated for a minute, knowing this would not be an easy scene to witness, but accepted his invitation. Photograph by Jane Rogers. NMAH It was a beautiful fall day with blue skies and cool, crisp air, much like September 11 had been. We drove up to the site, passing mini blinds tangled in the few trees that were left, and were struck by the sheer volume of paper. Sheets and sheets of financial documents and correspondence from all of the various offices that had once filled the World Trade Center littered the site. The damage to many of the surrounding buildings was severe and most were in need of major repair or demolition.
